name: CO2 laser blepharoplasty

lead: CO2 laser blepharoplasty gives the same eyelid reshaping as standard surgery, with a laser doing the cutting. People choose it for refreshed, smoother lids, and it can be paired with laser resurfacing of the fine wrinkles around the eyes.

The carbon dioxide laser vaporises tissue while sealing small blood vessels, giving a drier surgical field than a scalpel. Small side-by-side comparisons from the 1980s and 1990s report less bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, with no long-term difference in cosmetic result or scarring.

paras: A surgeon uses the laser in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery during upper or lower eyelid surgery, optionally adding resurfacing of the surrounding skin. Early recovery is described as easier with less bruising, and the final look is reported as similar to conventional technique.
General blepharoplasty risks apply. Published reports include a case of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty and cases of strabismus after cosmetic blepharoplasty.

angle.text: A CO2 laser takes the place of the scalpel to reshape eyelid skin and fat, sometimes with resurfacing of fine lines around the eyes. Small studies report less bleeding and bruising during recovery, with a similar final look.

lead: CO2 laser blepharoplasty is eyelid surgery in which a carbon dioxide laser is used as the cutting and coagulating instrument in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery [1][2]. People choose eyelid surgery to remove hooded or drooping upper-lid skin, reduce lower-lid bags, and give the eyes a more open, rested look; the laser variant is offered as a way to do the same operation with less bleeding and an easier early recovery [3][4]. It may be combined with laser resurfacing of the surrounding skin to treat periocular wrinkles [5].

Published reports from the 1980s and 1990s, mostly small series and paired side-by-side comparisons, describe less intraoperative bleeding and less early bruising and swelling with the laser, with no long-term difference in cosmetic result or scarring compared with conventional technique [2][6][1]. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled four comparative studies involving 133 patients, three of them split-face designs, and reported under its title that the CO2 laser improves early postoperative outcomes compared with conventional techniques [7].

Documented complications include a case report of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty [8]. Surgeons who favour the technique describe it as most useful when eyelid surgery is combined with resurfacing of the lid skin [9].
infobox: Upper and lower eyelid surgery; periocular resurfacing [5][10]

paras: The laser cuts tissue while cauterising small vessels, which is the basis of the claimed advantages: better control of bleeding and a clearer surgical field [2][1]. It can be used for upper and lower lid surgery, including transconjunctival lower-lid approaches, and for resurfacing periocular skin during the same operation [5][10]. A general encyclopedia account lists the cited benefits as less bleeding, shorter surgery, less bruising, swelling and pain, and notes some dispute about whether laser use counts as surgery [11].

Blepharoplasty is a long-established operation: the Roman writer Celsus described excising eyelid skin in the first century, and the term itself was introduced by Karl Ferdinand von Graefe in 1818, originally for repairing eyelid defects caused by cancer [11]. Upper blepharoplasty places an incision in the natural lid crease and removes excess skin, muscle or fat; lower blepharoplasty can be done through the skin below the lashes or through the inner surface of the lid with no external scar [11].

A clinical review of laser approaches notes that conventional blepharoplasty yields little improvement in several signs of periorbital aging, such as crow's feet, infrabrow and lower-lid wrinkling, crepey texture and pigment spots, which the author says can be improved by combining laser blepharoplasty with laser resurfacing [9]. Wikipedia also records historical disagreement over whether laser eyelid work counts as surgery, since the American College of Surgeons definition includes treatment by lasers [11].

A 1984 series of 40 patients with average 16-month follow-up described good control of bleeding and minimal postoperative bruising and swelling, with advantages and technical disadvantages discussed [2]. A 1987 paired comparison in 13 patients, laser on one side and cold steel with electrocautery on the other, found reduced operative time, bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, but no difference in cosmetic end result or scars at long-term follow-up [6]. A 1992 comparison in 10 patients used the same split-face design [1]. A 1990 review weighed advantages and disadvantages of the technique [12]. A 1994 study of 36 patients examined ultrapulse CO2 resurfacing of periocular skin together with transconjunctival laser lower-lid surgery [5]. A 2000 report described laser blepharoplasty with orbicularis/septum tightening and skin resurfacing as safe and advantageous [10].

Reviews describe the CO2 laser as cutting with limited surrounding thermal damage, giving incisions that heal with scarring comparable to traditional cold steel, while its hemostasis shortens surgery and lessens bruising and swelling [3]. A German-language review of upper lid surgery with the CO2 laser reports the clinic's experience with a device that incises and provides hemostasis together, in patients typically aged 40 to 60 [4]. A randomized split-face study of ten patients compared a free-beam CO2 laser with a diamond scalpel combined with a CO2 laser for upper-lid blepharoplasty [13].

A 1998 case report described necrotising fasciitis from group A streptococcus after laser blepharoplasty [8], and a 2003 report described acquired strabismus following cosmetic blepharoplasty in general [14]. The 1997 ASAPS/ASPRS Laser Task Force survey summarised complications and practice patterns for laser resurfacing and laser blepharoplasty among surgeons [15].

Beyond the 2026 meta-analysis [7], a 1998 survey summary from the ASAPS/ASPRS Laser Task Force collected practice patterns and complications among surgeons performing laser resurfacing and laser blepharoplasty [15]. Typical recovery after eyelid surgery in general involves bruising and swelling lasting several weeks [11].
CO2 laser blepharoplasty has been reported as a treatment for Morbihan disease, a chronic eyelid swelling condition [16].

Human studies consist of small case series and paired split-face comparisons: 40 patients [2], 13 patients [6], 10 patients [1] and 36 patients [5]. These report reduced bleeding, bruising and swelling with the laser but no long-term difference in cosmetic result versus scalpel surgery in the paired comparison [6]. No large randomised trials were found.
